3. The learned District Judge held that the testator was legally competent and mentally and physically fit and the will was executed bonafide by him and it was duly attested and registered. He however, found that as the testator was a rent-receiver the will was hit by Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 5. The only question that calls for our determination is whether the will in question is hit by Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was in operation when the will was executed on 23-5-56, but stood repealed on 29th Poush 1372 B.S. corresponding to 14-1-66 when the testator died. 

 6. When the will was executed Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stood as follows: 

 "9(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (1) of section 3, no rent-receiver specified in such notification shall, except with the previous permission of a prescribed authority, transfer his rights and interests in any estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy, to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease, or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means: 

 7. Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Ordinance No. XXVII of 1961 amended the above provisions and made certain additions thereto. Section 9 after amendment read as follows:- 

 "9(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (1) of section 3, no rent-receiver specified in such notification shall, except as provided in sub-section (1a), transfer his rights and interest, in any estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means without the previous permission of a prescribed authority." 

 (3) Nothing contained in the foregoing sub-section shall render void any transfer which, prior to the coming into force of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Ordinance, 1961, was not in contravention of any law for the time being in force and was legal and valid. 

 Subsequently by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, (Act No VI of 1964) Sections 9 to 9D were omitted: 

 "Section 9. as already pointed out, does not place any complete embargo on transfers of khas lands but merely restricts the mode of transfer, far, all that is necessary under this section is that the prior permission of the prescribed authority should he obtained for certain kinds of transfer. The intention of this section which was in the nature of an ad-interim provision, was clearly to prevent further complications before the preparation of the record of rights or the compensation assessment roll was undertaken. But even so, this section at no stage prevented the transfer by sale or mortgage of either agricultural or non-agricultural khas lands of the class retainable under sub-section (2) of section 20 of the Act if the land so transferred did not exceed ten standard bighas. This intention has now been made abundantly clear by the total repeal of the provisions section 9 to 9D by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act (Act No. VI of 1964) after the record of rights and compensation assessment rolls had been prepared."

 Section 144- Record of rights in SA and RS Khatian do not confer any title- Kabala deed prevails over record of rights. "

The plaintiffs also prayed for a permanent injunction. 

 5. The plaintiffs' case is that Abdul Kader was the owner of 22.5 decimals of land recorded in RS. Plot No. 5239. By a registered deed of gift No. 2329 dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3), he gifted the said 22.5 decimals of lands and other lands to his two daughters, namely Rowshan Banu and Hosne Banu in equal share. Rowshan Banu died leaving a daughter and a son who inherited her share in the lands. By a registered sale deed No. 3371 dated 27-4-1974 (Exhibit. 5), the heirs of Rowshan Banu sold the suit land consisting of 15 decimals, which was recorded in RS Plot No. 5239, to Abul Hossain. Hosne Banu by a registered sale deed No. 3083 dated 11-6-1974 (Exhibit. 4) sold lands including the land recorded in the RS Khatian No. 5239 to Abul Hossain. Thus, Abul Hossain became the owner of the lands including the suit land. The plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Abul Hossain by a registered deed No. 1698 dated 7-5-1987 (Exhibit. 7). Precisely, this is the chain of title of the plaintiffs. 

 11. Exhibit-3 is the foundation of the plaintiffs' case. It is noted that the defendants also raised objection as to admissibility of certified copies of sale deed dated 27-4-1974 (Exhibit. 5) and sale deed dated 7-5-1987 (Exhibit. 7) in evidence which also form part of the chain of title of the plaintiffs. The objections are recorded in the deposition sheet as well as on the back page of the Exhibited documents. 

 16. Under section 79 of the Evidence Act, a Court is bound to draw the presumption that a certified copy of a document is genuine and also that the concerned officer signed it in the official character which he claimed in the said document. But such a presumption is permissible only if the certified copy is substantially in the form and purported to be executed in the manner provided by law in that manner. In other words, if the certified copy is executed substantially in the form and in the manner provided by the law, the Court raises a rebuttable presumption in regard to its genuineness. The scope of section 79 was considered in Bhinka and others vs Charm Singh, AIR 1959 SC 960. In this case, three Courts rejected the certified copy of the record-of-rights on the ground that it was not genuine on the basis of not only the internal evidence furnished by the document but also on other evidence. In this case, neither the official diary of the Patwary, who was the authorised officer to issue certified copies of the record-of-rights, was produced before the Court to prove that the prescribed procedure was followed nor the extract noted in the diary to disclose that the Patwary made any note of payment as required by law. The Indian Supreme Court held that it cannot, therefore, be said that the certified copy was issued by the Patwary in substantial compliance with the provisions of law governing such issue. It follows that the Court is not bound to draw the presumption in regard to its genuineness. It was further held that even if there was any rebuttable presumption, it was so rebutted. 

 "A registered sale deed is the primary evidence of the interest sold. Under section 74(2) of the Evidence Act, 1882 public record of a private document like a sale deed when kept in the office of the Sub-Registrar to which the public generally have access falls within the category of public document and .a certified copy. of such a document can be adduced as a secondary evidence, though the reception of such evidence will be of a weak character in place of the registered document evidencing the sale.

That is the sum and substance of the submissions of the learned Senior Advocate Mr MI Farooqui. 

 "A writ of certiorari is maintainable only if it can be shown that the tribunal erroneously held that the property was illegally declared as abandoned property without admitting legal evidence or it has misconstructed the law. In other Words, a writ of certiorari does not lie for an erroneous decision in respect of a matter which is within the jurisdiction of the inferior tribunal. Unless such erroneous decision relates to anything collateral, an erroneous decision upon which might affect jurisdiction and the statute does not confer upon the tribunal final jurisdiction to decide such question. A writ of certiorari is maintainable only in a case where erroneous decision within it jurisdiction. Even if there is mere error of law that will not confer any power on the High Court Division to issue a writ of certiorari except where there is an error apparent on the face of the record that means, the error must be something more than a mere error. He added that the aforesaid Admitted facts has developed after the institution of the instant appeal and universal acceptance of abolishing jamindary system and declaring the projas as owners in the projabili properties, it is crystal clear that the Court of Wards and the land Reform Board who are appellants in this appeal have no locus-standi to claim over the projabili property cited in the projabili property Gazette (Annexure-2). He has pointed that the trial Court has also hold after discussing the said projabili property Gazette (Annexure-2) and also the compensation payment Gazette (Annexure-3) of the Bhawal Raj Estate, that the plaintiffs and other defendants became owners in possession of the suit properly by operation of law, i.e., the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The present appellants, the Court of Wards and the Chairman, Land Reform Board have filed the instant Is' Appeal No.12 of 2014. challenging the said findings of the trial Court connecting with the acquisition of rent receiving interest of the previous Jaminders, Bhawal Rajas in their projabili properties. In such, Circumstances the present plaintiffs respondents who became owners of the suit properties by operation of law, filed the present application for recording an order of abatement as per P.O. No.90 of 1972 after serving copy thereof upon the appellants learned Advocate. 

 14. Before enactment of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there was Zamindary System in the land Administration and Zamindar had two types of property, one projabili property i.e. land settled to the projas subject to payment of rent to the Zamindar and another, the khas property i.e. the property remained in possession of the Zamindar like his own house, garden, ponds etc. In the projabili property though the Zamindar had only rent receiving interest but in the name of realization of that interest/rent from the projas, the servants under the Zamindar (Paik Peyada) usually oppressed the projas/raiyats which shocked the then political leaders and social reformer for the abolishing the Zamindari System. Those political Leaders and Social reformer promised to the general public that if the country is liberated from British Rule they would abolish the Zamindari System and the projas under the Zamindar would be upgraded as Malik (owner) from the status of Projas. 

 15. Accordingly, when the India was divided in the year 1947, the erstwhile Government of the province of East Pakistan for abolishing the Zamindari System declaring the projas rights and title as owners had enacted the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the year 1950. 

 16. The provincial Government for giving effect the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in respect of the projabili property of the Zamindar/rent receiver remained under the management and custody of the court of Wards, the Government of the province of East Pakistan added Section 8(A) in the Court of Wards Act, 1879 by the Act No. X of 1951 stating as follows: 

 "If the rent-receiving interests of a ward in any estate under the charge of the Court are acquired under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, the remaining properties of such ward including khas lands under the charge of the Court shall continue to remain under its charge and shall be managed in accordance with the provisions of this Act, as if such ward were a disqualified proprietor of an estate." 

 The Government as per said modes and procedure firstly published a gazette notification under Section 3 of the said SAT Act, 1950 in the year 1952 (Annexure-A(1) describing therein the description of the projabili property in the column No.2 and the name and address of the Zamindar/rent Receiver in the column No. 1. 

 Before publication of the said projabili property gazette the Government had issued a notice under Section 3(A) and 4 of the said SAT Act, 1950 asking the Zamindar/rent Receiver to submit a list of projabili property remained under possession of their projas and khas property under their ownership and possession with a penal clause in case of failure to submit the list as asked for. 

 The Government after receiving of the said list from the concerned Zamindar both of projabili and khas properties had published a projabili property gazette in the year 1952 under Section 3 of the said SAT Act, 1950. So, the projas under the then Zamindar whether had /have no document connecting with the settlement as projas is very immaterial at least in deciding dispute in between the Zamindar and the projas. 

 17. After publication of the projabili property gazette under Section 3 by complying 3(A) and 4 of the said SAT Act, 1950, the Government had done the following acts: 

 "(a) Assessed the compensation against acquiring the Zamindari/rent receiving interest of the Zamindar under Section 33 of the SAT Act, 1950, which was commonly known as Compensation Assessment Roll (CA Roll). 

 (C) After payment of compensation to the Zamindar the then Government published a compensation payment gazette under Section 46E of the SAT Act, 1950 in the year 1956 declaring that the compensation assessed against acquisition of rent receiving interest of the Zamindar in the projabili property cited in the projabili property gazette published under Section 3 of the SAT Act, 1950 had been paid. 

 (d) After completing the aforesaid process for acquiring Zarnindari/rent receiving interest, the property cited in the projabili property gazette were recorded in the names of concerned projas upgrading them as owners in the khatian known as State Acquisition (S.A.) khatian after determining the land revenue under Section 24(1) of the SAT Act, 1950. As such, almost in all the S.A. khatian Section 24(1) of the SAT Act, 1950 was cited as the basis of determining land development tax payable by the new owners by operation of law to the new rent receiver, the Government." 

 18. After the independence of Bangladesh Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman as president of the country when found that the previous Zamindar were yet taking the advantage of loophole of the SAT Act, 1950 and thereby they were trying to make the said Act ineffective and meaningless by filing Civil Suits and other proceedings, he for protecting the projas who became owners by operation of law promulgated the President Order No. 90 of 1972 prohibiting the previous Zamindars/rent receivers from disturbing their previous projas whose properties had been cited in the projabili property gazette as follows: 

 "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E.B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Order No. III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect; and no court shall entertain, and no person shall bring, any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question." 

 Order No. 90 of 1972, which gives a clear mandate of law that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Ordinance No. III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect,- and no Court shall entertain and no person shall bring any fresh suit, appeal — application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question" 

 "With the publication of notifications under section 3 all rent-receiving interests including wakf and debuttor property stood acquired by and vested in the Government  after the notification issued under section 3 of the Act the status of the under raiyat became upgraded to that of raiyat. The rent receiving interests can be acquired even before the preparation of record of rights and publication of compensation assessment rolls'  with the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests by the government all intermediary interests disappeared and a person holding the land under the government becomes a "tenant", becomes a "raiyat" or a "malik" of the land recognized by the government. Consequently, the under-raiyat who actually holds the land becomes a tenant under the government. Superior land lord (i.e. the raiyat) of an under-raiyat by virtue of elimination of his rent-receiving interests disappears and the under-raiyat is upgraded to the status of a "raiyat".... record of rights prepared and finally published under section 144 cannot be varied by any authority and remedy of wrong entry if any lies with the appropriate court'  the property enlisted/ shown in the "projabili property" Gazette are the properties of "projas" who have been accepted as "owners" and the "rent receiving" interest whatsoever it had therein, of the jamindars all vested to the Government by operation of SAT Act, 1950." 

 After realizing their mistake, they firstly issued a Circular No.বি.আর.ঢাকা-৮১/২০০৩/৩২৪ dated 10.7.2014 under the signature of Mr. Raisuddin, the then Manager of Court of Wards, Bhawal Raj Estate cum Deputy Secretary of the Government of Bangladesh, stating that the Court of Wards as custodian of the Wards has no claim over the projabili properties as cited in the projabili property gazette published under Section 3 of the SAT Act, 1950 as per section 8(A) of the Court of Wards, 1879 and P.O. 90 of 1972 and also the judgments passed by the apex Court. Thereafter, the concerned Ministry of land had also issued a letter bearing Memo No.৩১.০০.০০০০.০৪২.৬৭.০৩২.১৫ dated 27.10.2015 and another letter bearing Memo NO. ৩১.০০.০০০০.০৪৬.৫৮.০১৯.১২-৭০ dated 02.02.2016 directing the Government servants engaged in the Court of Wards not to claim any sorts of right, title and interest in the projabili property cited in the projabili property Gazette in 1952. 

 27. According to the pleading of the plaint, the plaintiffs prayed for relief against the present appellants are that to declare that suit R.S. khatian No.500 in the name of the appellants are wrong. As a matter of facts both the learned Advocates admitted that the suit R.S. plot arises out of C.S. khatian No.107 was recorded rightly in the name of Mr. Kumar Rabindra Narayan Ray Chowdhury and others by Courts of Wards. It also admitted facts that at the time of the abolishing the Zamindari system the erstwhile East Pakistan Government had enacted the law namely: "The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the year 1950." 

 28. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, the learned Senior Advocate though argued that the appellant did not file the suit nor challenged the order of the acquisition rather filed the appeal against the judgment and decree of the trial Court according to the Code of Civil Procedure. It is true the appellants did not file suit but it cannot be argued on behalf of the appellants that they got the R.S. record of right in its name through purchase deed or on the basis of any other instrument claiming the same from the bonafide owner. Rather, if we have gone through the case law as well as the provision of law of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and P.O. 90 of 1972 as cited herein above then it would be crystal clear that the appellants challenged the judgment and decree by preferring the appeal, resultantly challenged the acquisition of the property as a Court of Ward in violation of the provisions of sections (3) A, 4 of the SAT Act-1950 read with the section 8(A) of the Court of Wards Act 1879 (Act No. X of 1951) and P.O. 90 of 1972.

full_judgment:
5.. During the trial both the parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence. From the side of the plaintiff many persons were initially examined as PWs and from the side of the defendants 7 persons were examined as DWs. The plaintiff Deity was represented by its Shebayet Mon Mohan Das, Baisbab and he examined himself as PW 1. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by a judgment and order dated 31-12-69, holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff opposite party had not succeeded in proving his alleged title to the suit land. Against the aforesaid judgment and order dated 31-12-69 the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 preferred First Appeal No.199 of 1970 on 23-4-70 in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and in the Memorandum of Appeal the plaintiff Deity was represented by Mon Mohan Das Baishnab upon whose death the plaintiff Deity was represented by Gopal Das Baishnab alias Kamal Das Baishnb. That first Appeal was heard by a Division Bench of the High Court Division and the same was allowed by the judgment and order dated 9-7-80 holding that without declaration that the sole decree obtained in Title Suit No. 331 was obtained by intimidation and undue influence therefore no relief could be given to the plaintiff opposite party and remanded the case back to the trial Court for giving opportunity to the parties to amend the plaint suitably and to bring on record the necessary elements to show that the sole decree obtained in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 was obtained by intimidation, undue influence and coercion and it was further observed that there was insufficient evidence as regards nomination of a person to hold the post of Shebayet in case a Shebayet died without a disciple as alleged in the plaint and kept the entire matter open for the trial Court to arrive at a decision in accordance with law. Against that judgment of the High Court Division a Civil Petition for leave to appeal No. 17 of 1981 was preferred by the defendant No. 1 alone and that application was summarily rejected by the Appellate Division by its order dated 23-1-81 and upheld the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. Ultimately, the record of the suit was sent back to the trial Court and the plaint was amended and additional written statement was filed by defendant No.1 and the opposite party No. 12, that is, defendant No.5(ka) who is son of late Sekandar Ali denying all material allegations made in the amendment petition. The opposite party Nos. 26-27 namely, Mahmud Ali and the Government of Bangladesh respectively who were added as defendant Nos.13 and 15 respectively also filed separate written statement denying all material allegations in the plaint. 

 7. In view of the pleadings of the parties the issues were recast and additional evidence from the side of the plaintiff opposite party No.1 as well as from the side of the opposite party No.26, that is, the defendant No.13 were also taken by the trial Court and on a review of the evidence and materials on record the trial Court decreed the suit vide its judgment and decree dated 17-11-86. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendant No. 1 that is, the present petitioner as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.29 of 1987 while the opposite party No. 26, that is, the defendant No. 13 preferred Title Appeal No. 40 of 1987 in the court of the learned District Judge, Sylhet and both the appeals upon transfer were heard analogously by the learned Assistant District Judge, First Court, Sylhet who disallowed both the aforesaid appeals by one and the same judgment and decree dated 30-8-92. The present petitioner that is, defendant No. 1, being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below preferred the instant revisional application and the present opposite party No. 26, that is, defendant No. 13, preferred another revisional application which is numbered as Civil Revision No. 3229 of 1992 and both the revisional applications relate to the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 30-8-92 and, as such, both the Rules were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment. 

 8. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the Rules, submits that the trial Court decided the issues in question without proper assessment of evidence on record. The learned Advocate further submits that the prayer is vague and unspecific and, as such, it is incapable of execution but the courts below overlooked that aspect of the case and erroneously decreed the suit finding title of the Deity in the suit land and for confirmation of possession also for recovery of possession from the portion of the suit land which is found to be in possession of the defendant No. 1 Jogendra. The third plank of attack made by Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that the trial Court in decreeing the suit did not consider the documentary evidence filed by the defendant petitioner except Ext. M and M(1) and that has caused miscarriage of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no specific averment either in the plaint or in their evidence as to when the plaintiff Deity was dispossessed from the suit land and there is also no averment that the plaintiff Deity was in possession of the suit land within twelve years from the date of dispossession and, as such, the instant suit is hit by both articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act but both the courts below misconceived the scope of the suit for possession and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The further submission of Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that neither of the courts below have considered Ext. O, a report of local investigation filed by the Advocate Commissioner in an earlier suit filed by the defendant No. 1 and the impugned judgment suffers from illegality on that score as well. The learned Advocate further submits that the judgment suffers from non-consideration of auction purchase particularly the date of delivery of possession. The learned Advocate emphatically submits that without framing any issue on the auction sale of the suit property the courts below committed an illegality in adverting to that aspect and decreeing the suit particularly in view of the fact that the defendant No. 3 took possession of the purchased land through court through execution case. The learned Advocate next submits that the impugned judgment is not tenable in law in view of the fact that it is asserted by the plaintiff Deity that the second schedule property was purchased out of the income of the Deity's property but there is no document of any kind to show that the second schedule property was purchased with the income of the Deity''s property and non-consideration of this aspect of the case also calls for interference with the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned judgment cannot be upheld in view of the fact that there is no finding by the courts below as to the existence of Deity and, as such, finding of the courts below that the suit property belongs to the Deity is absolutely erroneous and misconceived. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable without a prayer for declaration that the auction purchase made by defendant No. 3 is null and void but a paper transaction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The final submission of Dr Rahman is that it appears from the record that the present Shebayet in fact is not contesting in this revisional application and one Abdul Ahad who is allegedly a constituted attorney of the Deity is taking all steps in the courts and swearing the necessary affidavits as and when necessary and in fact it is this Abdul Ahad who is pursuing this litigation in the name of the Deity and it is also significant to note that none is coming from the Namasudra Community to make tadbir in this case on behalf of the Deity other than a Muslim and in this case a serious doubt arises on the whole case of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. 

 9. Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in both the Rules, submits that the plaintiff Deity has been successful in proving her case, title and possession in respect of the suit land and the alleged sole decree obtained by the defendant in their earlier title Suit No. 331 of 1966 along with the order in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 inasmuch as the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1 was not a party in those proceedings. The learned Advocate further submits that the alleged auction sale in favour of defendant No. 3 Sikandar Ali was also collusive and fraudulent and without covering any actual possession or title to him and the alleged sale is nothing but a mere paper transaction as per own admission of the alleged auction purchaser defendant No. 3 and his alleged subsequent transferee, the defendant No. 13 Mohammad Ali, whose deposition, on the other hand, will speak for itself to show that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction. The learned Advocate further submits that it is claimed by the defendant No. 1 that he is the adopted son of Kulok but there is no evidence on record in respect of ceremony of giving and taking him as adopted son and the defendant-petitioner has miserably failed to prove his adoption. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that there is no document to show that the suit property is a Dabottar property but Ext. 2 series, the CS records and Ext. 1 series, the name BAND. go to show that the suit property was recorded successively in the names of Baishnabs as disciple of Guru and there is no description of the father's name of the Baishnabs which consequently prove that the suit property belonged to the Deity for more than 100 years and these documents, that is, the CS Khatian and the Jama Bandi are the admitted documents and their genuineness arc not disputed by the defendant-petitioner. From Ext. 1 CS Khatian No. 251 it is found that Kulak Das Boishnab has been described as disciple of Joyram Boishnab and there is a homestead and from the materials coupled with the oral testimony of PWs conclusively established that the suit properties are not secular or personal properties of Kulak Das or of the defendant No. 1 but are dedicated properties and owned by the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1. The learned Advocate further submits that besides Exts. 1 and 2 Ties there are sufficient oral evidence on record to show that the suit property is debottor property inasmuch as PWs 4, 5 and 11 have categorically stated that from time immemorial the property is being used for the Sheba Puja of the Deity and the Puja offered by the Shebayets, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been able to prove by sufficient oral evidence that the suit property is being used for the Deity for a long period of over 100 years and the legal position is that if the property is used for a period of 50 years or more for performing Sheba Puja to a Deity that becomes Debottar property and in the instant case the oral evidence of the PWs coupled with the Ext. 1 and 2 series established it beyond any doubt that by long user for over long 50 years the suit property has become Debottor property and in that view of the matter, the trial Court rightly relied on the decision reported in 11 DLR 372,16 DLR (SC) 457; 24 DLR (SC) 36 and in addition to that the learned Advocate also refers to and relies on the decision reported in 36 DLR 47 and the case reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 797. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that the defendant No. 1 petitioner has been residing in portion of the outer house to the south of the Deity house as servant of the Shebayet and Mon Mohan Das was installed as Sebayet of the Deity and has been in possession of the entire suit land on behalf of the Deity and, as such, the defendant No. 1 has been in possession of a part of the ditch land, that is, the portion of the house he has been living in just as a servant and he had every right over the same. The learned Advocate next submits that there are overwhelming evidence on record to show that the alleged Solenama obtained in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and the Solenama executed in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were obtained by the defendant petitioner through coercion, threat, intimidation by filing series of cases against Mon Mohan Das one after another both Civil and Criminal. The learned Advocate further submits that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation and undue influence is clear from the fact that immediately thereafter the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Das instituted the instant suit for declaration of title of the Deity to the suit property and for further declaration that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence and not binding upon the plaintiff. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant suit both the courts concurrently found that the suit is not hit by article 142 or 144 and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has instituted the same well within the period of limitation and both the courts below on proper appreciation of materials on record arrived at a finding to that effect and question of limitation is a question of fact and since the concurrent finding of both the courts below is based on materials and evidence on record there is no scope for this court to interfere with that finding of fact which by no stretch of imagination is perverse. The learned Advocate repels the submission of Dr Rafiqur Rahman that there is no evidence on record to show that the second schedule property was purchased by Kulak Das with the income of the Deity's property inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 himself as PW 1 categorically admitted in his cross-examination that Kulak purchased the second schedule property from the income of the property which he got from Saran Das Boishnab his Guru, and the name of this Saran Das Boishnab also appears in the record of right as Boishnab as disciple of his Guru. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the admission of DW 1 himself that the second schedule property was purchased with the income of the property of Saran Das and the absence of any documentary evidence from the side of the plaintiff Deity that the second scheduled property was purchased by Mulak Das as Shebayet of the Deity is not fatal and this will have no material bearing on the title of the Deity in respect of the second schedule property as the defendant No. 1 has admitted that the property was purchased with the income of the first schedule property. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that no issue has been framed on the alleged auction purchase of the third schedule land but this story of auction purchase of the third schedule land was not in the original written statement which had earlier been filed by the defendant Nos. 1-3 jointly and it is only when the suit came back to the trial Court on remand the defendant No. 3 for the first time introduced the story of auction purchase and sale to defendant No. 13 who is opposite party No. 26 in Civil Revision No. 3228 of 1992 and petitioner in the next revision, namely, Civil Revision No. 3229 of 1992. The parties led evidence on the point and the courts below taking into consideration the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, have concurrently found that the auction sale is nothing but a sham transaction and the original defendant No. 3 did never get possession of third schedule land through court in execution proceeding arising out of the money suit and the appellate Court below taking into consideration the evidence of defendant No. 3 himself arrived at a positive finding that the alleged auction sale is nothing but a paper transaction and the defendant No. 2 did not acquire any right, title and interest in respect of the third schedule land and the alleged sale made by him to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 on 3-4-67 did not create any right, title and interest in their favour. The learned Advocate next submits that both the courts below rightly found that the suit is not barred by limitation inasmuch as mainly it is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and admittedly Kulak died on 25-12-1372. BS that is, some time in early part of 1965 and thereafter, the defendant No. 1 claiming himself as adopted son of Kulak filed a suit for permanent injunction, that is Title Suit No. 331 of 1966, and that suit was filed on 7-9-66 and it is alleged by the plaintiff Deity that the sole decree in suit No. 331 of 1966 has been obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation and undue influence and, as such, the Deity filed the present suit on 4-12-67 for declaration of its title and recovery of possession as well as for declaration that the sole decrees are null and void and obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation, and not binding upon the Deity and, as such, the suit was filed within two years from the date of death of Kulak. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant No.13 purchased the suit land on 3-4-67 and the defendant No. 13 also purchased some portion of the suit land from third schedule land from Sikandar on 3-4-67 and some other portions of the third schedule land from defendant No. 14 on 31-3-80 and the suit was filed well within 12 years from the date of this transaction and, in that view of the matter, the courts below did not commit any illegality and concurrently found that the suit is not barred by limitation under article 142 or 144 of the Limitation Act. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that none of the courts below considered Exhibit 0 but on a perusal of Ext. ''O'' it appears that this document, in fact, supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. In Ext. ''O'' it is stated that the defendant No.1 resides in the outer house which is situated within the suit land and it is also seen from Ext. ''O'' that there is a temple there though it has not been specifically mentioned that there is a Deity in the temple, but fact remains that a temple cannot be without any Deity and this shows that there was a Deity in the temple and on top of that there are oral evidences of the PWs to show that there is a Deity in the temple and Seba Puja is performed during Rath Jatra. Rash Jatra and Jhulan Jatra by the devotees and Shebayets of the Deity. The learned Advocate emphatically submits that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in the instant suit has paid ad-valorem court fees and prays for recovery of possession of the entire suit land and it is only after review of the evidence by the courts below they have found that the plaintiff Deity is not ousted from the entire suit land and is still in possession of the major portion of the suit land and, as such, decreed the suit declaring title of the Deity to the suit land, followed by confirmation of possession in respect of the land which are in possession of the Deity and decree for delivery of khas possession for that portion of the suit land where the defendant No. 1 is found to be in possession. Since the plaintiff has paid ad-valorem court fees on the entire suit land and since the plaintiff Deity has been successful in establishing her title to the suit land, it is immaterial in which portion or to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and since the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land, it is immaterial to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and the suit cannot be dismissed for not specifying the exact areas which is in possession of the defendant petitioner. The learned Advocate further submits that the omission to specify the exact area which is in occupation of the defendant petitioner is not fatal in the instant case, inasmuch as title of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been found in favour of the Deity and the suit is filed within the period of limitation. The learned Advocate next submits that the courts below did not commit any illegality in passing a decree for khas possession after evicting the defendant petitioner from the portion of the suit land which is found in his possession because under Order 7 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure a court is empowered to grant any relief to a party if it is found on consideration of the materials and evidence on record that the plaintiff has been able to establish his case to that effect and in support of his submission he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1963 (Punjab) 538, AIR 1942 (Pat) 247; AIR 1952 (SC) 47; 16 DLR 510; 14 DLR 307; AIR 1970(M) 40; AIR 1957 (All) 784. The learned Advocate finally submits that even if there be some lacuna in the impugned judgment this court sitting under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is competent to go through the records and the evidence adduced by the parties and on appraisal of the same if the court is of opinion that there are sufficient materials and evidence on record to ultimately sustain the impugned judgment, this court will not interfere with the same. The learned Advocate further submits that in an appropriate case, this court is entitled to enter into the merits of the case and decide the same finally, when the entire records are before it and this is the consistent view of our Appellate Division as has been taken in decisions, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 31; 43 DLR (AD) 78, 82, 125, and 44 DLR (AD) 98. The learned Advocate finally submits that on a perusal of the evidence and material on record, it is crystal clear that there are sufficient evidence and materials on record to show that the suit property actually belonged to the Deity opposite party No. 1 and the successive Boishnabs were managing the property as Shebayet of the Deity and applied the income of the suit property in performing Seba Puja of the Deity and therefore, the courts below did not commit any illegality in finding title of the Deity to the suit property and also in finding that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and that the suit is filed within time and the materials and evidence on record clearly supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. As such, there has been no error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice calling for any interference by this court. 

 11. Although in the normal course I should advert to the impugned judgment but in the instant case I would like to address myself about the judgment of the trial Court first because most of grievance agitated by Dr Rahman are in respect of the trial Court judgment. On a perusal of the trial Court judgment, it appears that the trial Court framed as many as 8 issues and there is no issue on the point of auction sale and this fact of auction sale was introduced by the original defendant No. 3 in the additional written statement, after remand of the suit to the trial Court. It further appears that no such issue was ever suggested by the defendant petitioners before the Court. Be that as it may, it would have been proper for the trial Court to frame an issue on that point but fact remaining that although no issue was framed on that point yet both the parties in the suit led evidence on that point and unfortunately, the trial Court did not advert to that aspect of the case and refrained from giving any finding on that point but that defect of the trial Court judgment has been cured by the impugned judgment inasmuch as the appellate Court below taking into consideration the evidence of defendant No. 3 arrived at a definite finding that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction. In this connection it may be stated that no doubt exhibit H the sale certificate dated 10-1-51 Ext, ''Ka'' Writ of delivery of possession dated 29-3-91 and exhibit. F-2 order confirming the delivery of possession show that after auction sale the delivery of possession of the property was duly handed over to the defendant No. 3 by the court in pursuance of the money execution case but the appellate Court below on consideration of the materials and evidence on record, particularly the evidence of the defendant No. 3, auction purchaser himself, came to a definite finding that the alleged auction sale and subsequent delivery of possession to the auction purchaser was collusively obtained beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff Deity and the Baishnabs and it is nothing but a paper transaction. In this connection, it may also be stated that the evidence of defendant No. 3 coupled with the evidence of defendant No. 1 also show that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a sham transaction. On top of that, it is alleged by the defendant No. 3 that he purchased the land in 1951 but it is admitted by him that he made no mutation after alleged purchase in 1951 and did not pay any rent in respect of this land since 1951 until 1967 when he transferred major portion of the auction purchased land to defendant Nos. 13 and 14. There is another aspect in this case that this defendant No. 3 did not however contest the case at the High Court before remand and it appears that in 1967 he sold 10½ bighas of land to the defendant Nos. 13 and 14. Thereafter 4½ bighas of land is still retained by him but in the instant suit after his death his heirs are not contesting the same even though they are brought on record. Thus it has been rightly found by the appellate Court below that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and that the same is collusive and obtained beyond the knowledge of the Baishnabs and the Deity and it is immaterial whether there is any prayer made by the plaintiff for setting aside the auction sale or not, because the auction sale is nothing but a sham transaction and has no existence in the eye of law. On top of that, it should be remembered that in the money suit or in the execution case, the Deity, that is, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, was not a party and, as such, that auction purchase is also not binding upon the Deity itself and here it may further be mentioned that the decree obtained in the money suit was an ex parte decree and the defendant No. 3 himself admitted in his evidence before the trial Court that he could not say how the summons of the suit was served on Kulak and what amount Kulak took as loan from him and these facts stare in the face of the defendant No. 3 and lend support to the finding of the appellate Court below that the auction purchase is, in fact, nothing but a paper transaction, collusively obtained by the defendant No. 3. 

 12. One of the grievances of Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that the trial Court without proper discussion of evidence decreed the suit. I had gone through the judgments of both the the courts. It is true that the trial Court in decreeing the suit did not refer to the evidence of all the PWs in detail but, nevertheless, on discussion of the relevant documents and materials and oral evidence and after proper consideration of the same arrived at a positive finding that the suit property is Debottor property and the suit land belongs to the Deity. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well it appears that the appellate Court below discussed about the evidence adduced by all the PWs and discussed about some of the documents and although did not discuss about the evidence of all the DWs, but on a perusal of the evidence adduced by the DWs vis-a-vis the evidence of the PWs and materials on record, concurred with the findings of the trial Court and on a perusal of the records I am of the opinion that there are sufficient evidence on record for both the courts below to arrive at a finding at which they have so arrived. Thus it cannot be said that the decision given by the courts below are not based on proper discussion of evidence on record. 

 13. The second plank of attack made by Dr Rahman is that the prayer is vague and unspecific. The plaintiff Deity did not specifically state in her plaint as to when and from what portion of the suit land she was dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 and, as such, the decree passed by the courts below is not sustainable in law. It appears that the instant suit is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the plaintiff has paid ad valorem court-fees on the entire suit land, and initially prayed for recovery of possession of the entire suit land after evicting the defendant No. 1 from the suit land. Both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land except certain portion where the defendant No. 1 lives in the homestead plot and, as such, decreed the suit is favour of the plaintiff and passed a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defendant No. 1 from that portion of the suit land where he is found in possession. The case of the defendant No.1 is that he is in possession of the entire suit land, where as the case of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is that he is in permissive occupation of the suit land and he has no right, title and interest in the suit land and the defendant No.1 admittedly was brought to the suit land by Kulak. The further case of the plaintiff is that he was brought to the suit land by Kulak, the then Shebayet of the Deity and he used to perform the domestic work. The dispute arose between the parties only after the death of Kulak, when the defendant No. 1 claimed himself as the adopted son of Kulak and claimed the suit property as personal property of Kulak and he filed Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and thereafter, the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Boishnab filed the instant suit in 1967. It is also admitted fact that Kulak Das died on 25th Chaitra, 1372, BS. It thus appears that the plaintiffs brought suit within 2 years from the date of death of Kulak and when the plaintiff No. 1 raised his claim to the suit property as his own property as heir of Kulak. It has already been noted that the appellate Court below on due consideration of the material and evidence on record found that the auction purchase is a sham transaction and that did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the defendant No. 3 in respect of land of schedule 3. Besides defendant No. 3 sold the suit land in 1967 to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 and defendant No. 13 purchased some portion of the third schedule land from defendant No.14 in 1980. It is, thus crystal clear that the finding of the appellate Court below that the suit is not barred by limitation is borne out by sufficient materials and evidence on record. Since the suit is a suit for declaration of title followed by recovery of possession both the courts below, in my opinion, did not commit any illegality by passing a decree declaring title of the Deity to the suit land followed by claim of possession in the suit land and also by passing a decree for khas possession of that portion of land which is found to be in occupation of the defendant No. 1. Since the plaintiff Deity has paid ad-valorem court fees for the entire suit land, if her title is established in the suit land she is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land and since she is already in possession of major portion of the suit land, she is entitled to get recovery of possession of that portion of land which is in possession of defendant. In that view of the matter I do not find any substance in this submission of Dr Rahman. 

 14. Another plank of attack made by Dr Rahman is that in decreeing the suit the trial Court did not discuss the documentary evidence of the defendants except Ext. M and M-1. But during the course of argument he failed to point out what are the other documentary evidence, non-consideration of which vitiated the judgment. It appears from perusal of the trial Court judgment that besides Ext. M and M-1 he has also considered Ext. C series and B series along with Ext. 1 series and 2 series and the oral evidence of PW 1 and PW 4, and on perusal of the appellate Court judgment it appears that although he has not referred to all the documentary evidence in detail but it appears that he has considered the oral and documentary evidence adduced by both the parties and after considering the entire evidence adduced by both the parties the appellate Court below arrived at a positive finding that it is true that there is no documentary evidence to show that the suit land belongs to Deity plaintiffs or that the suit lands were recorded in the record of rights in the names of the Baishnabs as Shebayets of the Deity, but taking into consideration the evidence and circumstances of the case, the appellate Court below came to a finding that for three generations the suit lands were recorded in the record of rights in the names of Baishnabs, as disciples of other Boishnabs, which points out that the suit land is nothing but a dedicated property and the Baishnabs were holding that property as Shebayets of the Deity. Besides, Ext. B dated 24-11-1908 and Ext. 5, a registered deed of lease dated 17-6-1935 also show that both Saran Das and Kulak Das were described as Shebayets of the Deity and their occupation was shown as servant of the Deity. In that view of the matter the concurrent finding of both the courts below that the suit land belonged to the Deity plaintiffs opposite party No. 1 is also backed by sufficient materials and evidence on record; I have already pointed out that the instant suit was filed within 2 years from the date of death of Kulak. As such the omission of the plaintiff Deity to mention as to the date of possession and dispossession in respect of the suit land is immaterial and does not have any bearing on this suit because admittedly the defendant No. 1 was brought to the suit land by Kulak and during his lifetime he used to live with Kulak. It is only after the death of Kulak the defendant No.1 claimed himself to be the adopted son of Kulak and also claimed the property as personal property of Kulak but facts remain that the defendant petitioner No. 1 has miserably failed to show that he was the adopted son of Kulak Das Baishnab. It is clear from Ext. 4(Ka) dated 10-6-61 and ext. 8 dated 18-11-66 that defendant No. 1 has been described in these documents as son of one Kanak, his natural father and not of Kulak, the alleged adopted father. Besides, from the Solenama Ext. "E" which relates to Title Suit No. 331 of 1966, it appears that there is mention of Akhrabari and the Deity Radha Krishna and that they are the Boishnabs but it is stated that the property is not being claimed as the property of Deity. It thus appears that both the courts below rightly arrived at a finding as to the title of the Deity to the suit land. 

 15. One of the main grievance of Dr Rahman is that there is total non-consideration of the fact that delivery of possession of the third schedule land was given to defendant No.3 through court in pursuance of auction sale. It is true the trial Court did not advert to that ex parte auction sale but nevertheless the appellate Court below after taking into consideration the relevant averments made by the parties in their pleadings vis-a-vis the evidence adduced by the parties on that point arrived at a definite finding that no actual delivery of possession was ever given to the defendant No. 3 in pursuance of the ex parte auction sale and that was a sham transaction. I am of the view that the suit would not fail in the absence of any prayer for declaration that the auction purchase is null and void, collusive, inoperative, a mere paper transaction and not binding upon the plaintiff because it has been found by the appellate Court on proper scrutiny of the materials and evidence on record that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and the same was collusively obtained by defendant No. 3. It has already been noted that although no issue on auction purchase was framed by the trial Court but the parties were conscious about the plea of alleged auction sale and both the parties adduced their evidence on the point and the appellate Court below after taking into consideration the evidence adduced by both the parties arrived at a finding that the alleged auction sale is a sham transaction and in that view of the matter I am of the opinion that since the title of the plaintiff Deity has been found in favour of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, omission on the part of the plaintiff to pray for declaration that the alleged auction purchase is null and void can not have any bearing on the merits of the suit. 

 16. Another major point of argument of Dr Rahman is that although it is claimed by the plaintiff Deity that second schedule land has been purchased with the income of the dedicated property but there is no documentary evidence to show that the schedule property was purchased with the income of the Deity's property. It is true that documentary evidence is wanting in this case on that point but there are oral evidence to show that the second schedule property was purchased by Saran and Kulak during their time as Shebayets with the income of the Deity''s property and nobody other than DW 1 himself also admitted in his cross examination Kulak Das purchased second schedule land with the income of property of Saran Das Boishnab. Thus, it appears to me that the absence of any documentary evidence to show that the second schedule property was acquired with the income of the Deity's property is not fatal in the instant case inasmuch as there is unimpeachable oral evidence to show that the second schedule land was acquired with the income of the Deity's property and it further appears from Ext. 1 (B) that the second schedule land is also recorded in the name of Kulak as disciple of Saran Das Boishnab which indicates the property as a dedicated one and not as secular or personal property because if it had been his personal property then his name would have been recorded as Kulak Das with his father's name. 

 18. From a close scrutiny of both the judgments it appears that on consideration of oral evidence coupled with the documentary evidence they have arrived at a concurrent finding that the suit property belongs to the Deity plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and 3 successive Baishnabs were, in fact, Shebayets of the Deity and this observation leads to the irresistible conclusion that there was a Deity in existence otherwise how the property could belong to Deity. Besides there are evidence adduced by the PWs namely, PWs 1, 3, 4 and 11 who in a voice stated that there is a Deity installed in the Akhrabari in the suit land and the Shebayets used to perform Seba Puja, namely, Rath Jatra, Rash Jatra and Jhulan Jatra and other Sectional Festivals and it is further noted by the learned appellate Court below that the oral evidence on this point is unshakable and the evidence adduced by the PWs cannot be brushed aside on any grounds and the trial Court, as well, categorically observed that he did not find any reasons to disbelieve the testimony of PW 1, one of the Shebayets, and PW 4, so there are sufficient evidence on record to show that there is a Deity in the Akhrabari within the suit land. In this connection we may also refer to Ext ''O'' a report of Advocate Commissioner filed in connection with earlier suit in respect of the self same property filed by defendant No. 1 himself and Ext ''O'' shows that there is a temple in the suit land. On top of that even the alleged Solenama of Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 Ext ''E'' also shows that there is a Akhrabari and Deity Rada krishna, so, in my opinion, there are overwhelming evidence on record to show that there is a Deity in the suit land in the Akhrabari namely, Radha Krishna Bigraha installed by the Baishnavs of the locality long long ago.

full_judgment:
4. The defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 7 to 9 also have filed written statement to the effect that they have been owning and possession the 0.54 acres of land from plot No. 360 by growing seasonal crops and they got the properties from the predecessors by way of inheritance and they have appointed one Md Moser Ali as their Attorney for maintenance of their property amounting to 3.23 acres of land including 0.52 acres of the suit land. But their names were not recorded in the SA Khatian for which they have filed another suit for declaration of title being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj against the plaintiffs-appellant-respondent-opposite party and while this defendant-opposite party petitioner No. 1 came to know that suit for declaration has started this defendant-petitioner filed a petition under Order I rule 10 for adding them as party in the aforesaid suit and the learned court was pleased to add them as party in that suit being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993. After conclusion of the trial the learned Court was pleased to dismiss the suit on contest and plaintiff filed an appeal against the said judgment and decree which is now pending before the court of Additional District Judge. 

 5. The trial Court after taking deposition of 6 witnesses for the plaintiff and 2 witnesses for the defendant and Exhibits and after considering the exits have dismissed the suit for permanent injunction and against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1-6 filed appeal before the learned District Judge and on transfer to the learned Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayangonj for disposal, the court after considering the evidence on record allowed the appeal against which the defendant-respondent- petitioner preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule. 

 6. Mr Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, submits that the trial Court after hearing the parties and the deposition and considering the Exhibits since found possession of the petitioner dismissed the suit which is very much in accordance with law against which the plaintiff-appellant-opposite parties have preferred appeal and the appellate Court without discussing the evidences allowed the appeal thus occasioned failure of justice. He further submits that both the plaintiff and the defendant though claimed the property by way of pattan but no pattan was produced before the court, RS was prepared in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiff and defendant. The petitioner has purchased by 3 registered deeds (Exhibits GH) on different dates and there was mutation case being No. 174 of 1986 and has been paying rent to the Government which are marked as Exhibit A series and paid rent up to 1991 and referred 28 DLR (AD) 61 and 32 DLR 252 wherein it has been stated Record of Right is not a document of title. It does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence it may support evidences of title. By itself, it is not an evidence of title "and it has been referred in 32 DLR 252 that Record of Right is evidence of present possession-Registered Kabala evidence of title. The records of rights of the Government which at best are evidence of possession at the time when such records are prepared and not an evidence of title as such this is a well-established principle of law. A registered Kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is canceled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit." He has further referred 43 DLR 226 "There is no specific area or demarcation of the land allegedly encroached by the defendants- opposite parties, in such a case no order of temporary injunction can be granted" and in this connection he has referred schedule 'A' description of the plaint where the boundary was not specifically mentioned and where there was no specific demarcation of the plot. The plaintiff-opposite party cannot claim for an injunction or is not entitled to have injunction. The appellate Court while disposing of the appeal did not consider this very aspect rather considered the dakhilas as produced by the plaintiff (marked as Exhibit 6) and the rent receipt to the government (marked as Exhibit 5) in this connection. He has referred 30 DLR (SC) 41 "the private document made an exhibit on its formal proof, presumption as to its writing-question of its genuineness is a question of fact" and he submits that the Exhibit 6 are all private documents and the burden of proof is on him to prove his genuineness of the rent receipts which were not at all proved. Thus the appellate Court being the final court of fact should have considered all these aspects for which he is not entitled thus occasioned an error in the decision required to be interfered by this court. 

 8. I have gone through the judgments of both the courts below and also Exhibits as filed by both the parties. Admitted fact is that the CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Jagadish and Ashutosh from where the plaintiff claims the ownership but the pattans were not produced by plaintiff and defendant before the court though RS was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff and defendants. The plaintiff produced some dakhilas and also rent receipts i.e. Exhibit 5 which appeared to have been paid on 16-3-1980 and Exhibit 5 Ka is paid in 1969 in the name of Tayab Khan and Exhibit 6 series are the dakhilas given by the jaminder and the defendants have also filed rent receipts of the government which were marked as Exhibit A series and admitted position is that he paid rent up to 1991. The defendants have mutated and submitted some documents of that purchase deed of different dates i.e. 12-3-1979 and 5-12-1979. The dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff are the private documents and that are ie, to be proved by the scribe, the signatures are to be compared which were not considered by the lower appellate Court. These private dakhilas are yet to be proved and it is referred in 35 DLR 129 "that dakhilas are private documents and it would not carry any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of any entry in the record of rights under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It appears that both the parties have adduced rent receipts and the petitioner has paid rent up to 1991 and there was mutation though the mutation proceeding is under challenge in the appeal and, according to decision 35 DLR (AD) 216, rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. The petitioner has submitted certain rent receipts marked as Exhibit A series which were not considered by the learned appellate Court. Though it is a question of fact based on finding and is proved and this aspect since not discussed by the learned appellate Court, I find substance in this Rule. Since rent receipts are evidence of possession and collateral evidence of title and in a suit for permanent injunction where the plaintiff did not mention the boundary of the specific plot and there is no specific demarcation, in that view of the matter, granting injunction in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained. 

 Send down the lower court records at once.

full_judgment:
3. The plaint case, in short, is that Jadunath Sarker and Sitesh Chandra Biswas were owners in possession as 'Korfa' tenants in equal share in said 36 decimals of land under one rent receiver, Protap Chandra Das Gupta and said Korfa tenancy was finally recorded in CS Khatian No. 124/20 in the name of Jadunath Sarker. While they were thus in possession by a registered deed of sale being No. 1612/38 dated 10-8-38 they transferred 12 decimals out of said 36 decimals of land to one Swadesh Ranjan Sarker and delivered possession to him. 

 4. Thereafter, Swadesh Ranjan Sarker transferred said 12 decimals of land to Md Abdul Wahed minor represented by his father Abdul Majid Sarker and Mohammad Rafiqul Islam. minor represented by his father Raj Mohammad Sarker by registered deed of sale being 7902 dated 21-3-53 and delivered possession to them. They also purchased 17½ decimals of land from the said plot. Accordingly, the names of Abdul Wahed and Rafiqul Islam were correctly recorded in the SA Khatian No. 184. 

 26. Both the suits were tried together and disposed of by one judgment. One set of evidence was recorded in the subsequent suit with reference to the parties therein. 

 31. On behalf of the appellant, Mr. Mahbubey Alam. learned Senior Advocate, took us through the record. and submitted that Mokhlesur Rahman actually first acquired the land in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and then made the construction out of his own money. Farida Rahman had no independent source of income as borne out by the evidence on record. Learned Joint District Judge fell in error in shifting the onus upon Shamsul Haque to prove 'Benami' transaction and holding that Farida Rahman acquired the land and constructed the house by her own money. 

 37. We find two sisters Luna and Dana living in England are fighting their uncle. Shamsul Haque and, to some extent, father Mukhlesur Rahman for their rights in the suit property left by their mother, Farida Rahman. How greed and hunger for property and money can come in the way to natural love, affection and care and ultimately, spoils all beauties of paternal love, care and duty is one of the finest examples set in the instant appeals. For clarity, we shall describe the parties with reference to their relationship. 

 44. The sale deed being No. 42106 dated 13-12-67 purchasing 12 decimals of land stands in the name of Farida Rahman. The consideration appears to be Taka 5,000. There is no dispute about the title of the vendors. Then, by order dated 20-1-69 passed in mutation case No 742/68-69 the record of rights was mutated in the name of Farida Rahman and since then rents were paid in her name. After construction of the house, municipal holding was created and electric and water connections, etc were all taken in her name. All papers revenue, tax, rates, etc stand in the name of Farida Rahman. 

 46. Accordingly, the record of rights stands again mutated in the names of Luna and Dana. All records relating to revenue, tax and utility services were accordingly mutated in the names of Luna and Dana. At no point of time from 1967 to 2000 when he deposed, Mokhlesur Rahman ever claimed any right or interest either over the land or the house. These are not disputed. 

 57. So, that is all the evidence that could have been adduced by Shamsul Haque in support of his case of 'Benami'. It should not however miss our attention that in 1998, Shamsul Haque for the first time claimed that in 1967 his brother Mukhlesur Rahman purchased the land in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and got the house constructed thereon through his father-in-law Hamiduddin Ahmed, Mukhlesur Rahman for the first time in his written statement filed in Court on 13-8-98 and deposition recorded on 6-2-2000 claimed that he first purchased the land and then got the house built thereon by his own money. Consistent case of two brothers is that Mukhlesur Rahman sent money for the price of the land as well as the cost of building to Hamiduddin Ahmed. But none of them tried to tender any evidence whatsoever on such transfer of fund to said Harniduddin Ahmed. There is practically no evidence at all of sending any fund to Hamiduddin by Mukhlesur Rahman. 

 62. In such circumstance and on the evidence on record, we do not have any hesitation to say that Shamsul Haque hopelessly failed to discharge the burden of proving the sale dated 13-12-67 was a 'Benami' and learned Joint District Judge therefore committed no error in rejecting the case of ' Benami'.
